title: Overlapped pipeline: decode-first handoff and micro-batch heuristics
content:
Summary:

This is a working sketch for a hybrid prefill/decode pipeline that lets us overlap prefill work with early decode tokens for interactive streams while preserving deterministic semantics and reasonable unit cost. Goal is lower p99 latency for streaming responses (especially for short continuations) without blowing up peak GPU memory or increasing token cost too much.

Context / problem statement:
- Current prefill-then-decode model guarantees correctness (all KV state present before any decode) but increases tail latency for streams where the prefill is large (long contexts, many cached prefixes).
- Pure interleaving (decode tokens while prefill in background) risks missing KV keys for attention computation -> incorrect outputs or expensive rework.
- We need a heuristic that: (a) allows fast start of streaming decodes for high-priority interactive requests, (b) keeps micro-batching efficiency for throughput, (c) bounds memory and re-computation cost.

Design principles / constraints:
- Determinism: If we promise identical output for non-streaming and streaming modes, we must ensure decode sees the same attention state as post-prefill scenario. In practice we may accept small differences for explicit "low-latency" mode (documented).
- Bounded rework: If a decode token used incomplete KV and later needs correction, re-run cost must be capped and chargeable/observable.
- Resource isolation: Avoid a single overloaded prefill blocking many cheap decodes.
- Prefer fast-path kernels when batch size is small (decoder-only or fused decoder attention kernels).

Proposal overview (Decode-first handoff with staged KV readiness):
1) Classify incoming request at admission: priority label = {interactive, background, batch} based on headers / route / SLA / user-specified.
2) Schedule a short prefill phase that populates a minimal working set of KV entries required for first N decode tokens (N small, e.g., 1-4 tokens) — call this the "starter prefix". This is constructed by scanning prefix lengths and heuristics (see below).
3) Begin decode on a fast-path using the starter prefix KV. Meanwhile continue prefill to fill full KV for remaining context asynchronously in same GPU or different shard depending on scheduling policy.
4) If during async prefill we discover that decode ran ahead of available attention keys and produced tokens that would have used missing keys, we either:
   - Option A (preferred for interactive): mark these tokens as "speculative" and attach metadata. Once full-prefill completes, verify determinism (re-run decode for affected time-window). If mismatches, emit correction messages + telemetry and (optionally) replay tokens to client.
   - Option B (strict): stall decode until full-prefill completed (fall back to existing behavior for non-interactive / high-consistency routes).

Starter prefix heuristics:
- Use token-likelihood and k-length heuristic: compute approximate receptive field: if average reply length <= L_small, prefill only most recent M tokens of context plus first attention block. Typical defaults: M=128 or 0.25 * context_len, whichever is smaller.
- For LLMs with local attention patterns (sliding window), we can avoid filling farther KV entries beyond the sliding window. Plug model metadata to inform these decisions.
- Use recent-keystream hotness: if we have prefix-level KV cache hit statistics, prefer cached regions for starter.

Micro-batching and windowing:
- Admission groups requests into micro-batches by a short window Wms (default 6ms) or a max batch size. For interactive high-priority streams, use lower W and smaller max batch to favor latency. For background/bulk, allow longer W to increase throughput.
- When mixing starter-prefill and decode in same GPU slot, schedule tasks as: prefill(starter) -> decode(first tokens) -> continue prefill(remaining) -> decode(continue). This preserves short critical-path decode while enabling batching for the bulk prefill work.
- Batch coalescing rule: if an interactive stream arrives and there is an ongoing large prefill batch, we may run the interactive starter prefill on a separate fast lane or steal headroom from existing batch if resource permits. This prevents head-of-line blocking.

Stream priority scoring (how to pick who goes first):
score = base_priority + sla_bonus + small_input_bonus - est_prefill_cost_penalty
- base_priority derived from route plan.
- sla_bonus from SLA tier (enterprise customers, low-latency routes get positive).
- small_input_bonus: shorter prefill contexts get preferencing; decodes that likely finish in <K tokens favored.
- est_prefill_cost_penalty: estimated GPU time to prefill full context reduces score.
Scheduler picks top-N streams for starter-prefill decode-first path on each GPU.

Kernel selection rules:
- If post-starter decode will be small-batch (<4 streams concurrently), select low-latency decoder kernels (fused rotary, merged matmuls) that optimize single-stream throughput.
- For larger batched prefill operations, select batching-optimized kernels (cuBLAS/flash attention fused graph).
- Provide hook for runtime to switch kernel sets mid-run (fast path for first tokens, then fallback to throughput kernels). We must checkpoint and adapt KV layout to avoid expensive reformatting; prefer kernels that share base layout.

KV cache strategy and sharding:
- KV is divided into three operational zones per model shard: starter-KV, streaming-KV (growing with decode), and archival-KV (full context).
- Starter-KV is kept resident in the local GPU memory and populated quickly. It is small by design.
- Streaming-KV grows as we emit tokens; we append entries in-place.
- Archival-KV may be spilled to host memory or separate GPU pool during large contexts; migrate back to GPU if further attention windows touch that region.
- Sharding policy: allow opportunistic sharding where a heavy prefill for one request can be placed on a different shard if cross-shard attention routing supports it (tradeoff: cross-shard attention costs).

Consistency and determinism model (modes):
- Strict mode: stall decode until full prefill complete — deterministic identical outputs to offline runs. Default for enterprise strict routes.
- Best-effort low-latency mode: speculative decode allowed. Operator-visible telemetry includes speculative-token-rate, re-run-rate, correction-rate. We surface these as metrics and tie to billing or SLA.

Cost accounting & observability:
- Track work units: starter-prefill ops, full-prefill ops, speculative-replay ops. Expose on per-request and per-token basis so product can reason about unit economics.
- New dashboards: speculative-replay per route, average speculative latency savings, GPU-seconds saved vs baseline full-prefill.
- Instrument kernel switches and memory migrations (events in trace).

Safety nets and backpressure:
- If speculative replay ratio for a model or route goes above threshold (e.g., >5%), auto-escalate to stricter starter-prefill heuristics or fall back to strict mode.
- Backpressure: if prefill backlog length > X, deprioritize new low-priority starters and route to dedicated background pool.

Experiments to run (A/B + alpha on infra):
- Metric set: p50/p90/p99 start-token latency, end-to-end latency, speculative-replay-rate, GPU-seconds per response, memory peak.
- Experiment 1: baseline vs starter-prefill N=2 tokens, W=6ms, interactive weight=2. Observe latency improvements on short streams.
- Experiment 2: kernel-switching enabled vs disabled (measure CPU/GPU kernel overheads).
- Experiment 3: aggressive spilling of archival KV to host vs keep-on-GPU. Measure reactivation costs.

Implementation plan (phases):
- Phase 0: prototype mode in runtime test harness. Implement starter-prefill path, speculative token tagging, and simple replay capability.
- Phase 1: add scheduler scoring and micro-batch windowing knobs in infra. Add telemetry.
- Phase 2: kernel switching & KV zone API; integrate with model catalog metadata for attention patterns.
- Phase 3: enterprise-safe flags, per-route strictness, autoswitching based on telemetry.

Open questions / tradeoffs (notes):
- How to compute minimal starter prefix accurately for long-range transformers (sparse/ALiBi)? Model metadata needed.
- Cross-shard prefill: cheaper to run on spare GPU vs pay cross-attention cost? We need cost model.
- Client UX: if corrections happen post-speculation, do we stream a correction delta or full resend? UX team input required.
- Billing: do we bill replay work separately or fold into total token cost? Product decision.

TODO / immediate next steps:
- Add simple simulation harness to replay historical traces and simulate starter-prefill vs full-prefill to estimate replay rates. (Owner: Daniel)
- Add new metrics to runtime traces: speculative_flag per token, prefill-phase latency, kernel-switch events. (Owner: Marco)
- Draft PR for starter-prefill protobuf change to tag tokens and backfill metadata. (Owner: Aisha)

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally experimental; many defaults are heuristics. Looking for feedback on starter prefix sizing, acceptable replay thresholds, and which routes should be conservative by default.
- If we want zero-diff determinism for all customers, we must have strict-mode default and treat speculative as opt-in. That reduces latency wins to only opted-in routes.
